cls: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (L- and T-type)
pharm: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that blocks both L-type and T-type calcium channels, lowering blood pressure with renoprotective and heart-rate-neutral effects.
quick: 20-40 mg once daily after breakfast; may increase to 60 mg once daily
Take after a meal (typically after breakfast)
Generally well tolerated; T-type blockade may be renoprotective - use with caution
Blood pressure, heart rate, peripheral edema, liver enzymes
summary: Efonidipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker marketed mainly in Japan and parts of Asia (not FDA-approved) for hypertension and angina pectoris. Unlike most dihydropyridines it blocks both L-type and T-type calcium channels. T-type channel blockade dilates both afferent and efferent renal arterioles, which may reduce intraglomerular pressure and offer renoprotection, and tends not to cause reflex tachycardia. It is usually taken once daily after a meal. As with other dihydropyridines, peripheral edema, flushing, and headache can occur.

dosage.d: 20-40 mg once daily after breakfast; may increase up to 60 mg once daily based on response
dosage.n: Per Japanese prescribing information; not FDA-approved

dosage.d: 40 mg once daily (some regimens 20 mg twice daily) after meals

admin: Take after a meal, usually after breakfast
Swallow with water; take at about the same time each day
Titrate based on blood-pressure response and tolerability
Monitor for ankle/leg swelling and dizziness
Do not stop abruptly in anginal patients - taper under guidance
moa: Efonidipine is a dihydropyridine that blocks voltage-dependent calcium channels of both the L-type and the T-type. L-type blockade in vascular smooth muscle reduces peripheral resistance and lowers blood pressure, as with other dihydropyridines. Additional T-type channel blockade dilates both afferent and efferent renal arterioles (lowering intraglomerular pressure) and suppresses the rise in heart rate seen with pure L-type agents, giving a heart-rate-neutral and potentially renoprotective profile. It may also modestly suppress aldosterone secretion.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to efonidipine or dihydropyridines
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy (per Japanese labeling)

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established; the manufacturer advises against use in pregnant women or those who may be pregnant. Use only if no safer alternative and the benefit clearly justifies the risk.
lact: Safety during breastfeeding has not been established and excretion into milk has been reported in animals; avoid use or discontinue breastfeeding during therapy.
renal: Efonidipine is generally well tolerated in renal impairment, and its T-type channel blockade dilating both afferent and efferent arterioles may reduce intraglomerular pressure (potentially renoprotective). Nonetheless, use with caution and monitor renal function.
hepatic: Efonidipine is metabolized in the liver; use with caution in hepatic impairment and monitor liver enzymes, as hepatic dysfunction has been reported.

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors - may increase efonidipine levels and hypotension
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) - may reduce efficacy
Cimetidine - may increase efonidipine plasma levels
interactions.food: Take after a meal; grapefruit juice may increase levels (CYP3A4) - avoid.
interactions.alcohol: May enhance blood-pressure lowering and dizziness; limit.
interactions.diagnostics: May modestly lower aldosterone; no characteristic lab interference.

counsel: Take this medicine after a meal, usually after breakfast, at the same time each day
Ankle swelling, flushing, or headache may occur - tell your doctor if troublesome
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness when you start treatment
Do not stop suddenly if you take it for angina - your doctor will guide tapering
pk: Blood-pressure-lowering effect within a few hours of dosing
Peak plasma concentration approximately 1.5-2 hours after an oral dose
Elimination half-life approximately 3-4 hours (effect prolonged due to high membrane affinity)
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - marketed mainly in Japan and parts of Asia (data from Japanese prescribing information / literature, not openFDA)
Dual L- and T-type calcium channel blocker - distinguishes it from standard dihydropyridines
Dilates both afferent and efferent renal arterioles, lowering intraglomerular pressure (potential renoprotection, useful in proteinuric/diabetic nephropathy)
Heart-rate-neutral - little reflex tachycardia compared with pure L-type agents
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not take two doses together.
overdose: Overdose may cause marked hypotension and reflex changes in heart rate. Management is supportive: place the patient supine with legs raised, give IV fluids and vasopressors as needed, and monitor cardiac function. Intravenous calcium may help counter calcium channel blockade. Dialysis is unlikely to be effective owing to high protein binding.
